content: Mineral water is a type of water that contains minerals or other dissolved substances, which can influence its taste or provide therapeutic benefits. These dissolved substances may include salts, sulfur compounds, and gases. Mineral water is often naturally carbonated, giving it an effervescent quality. It can either occur naturally or be artificially prepared. Historically, mineral water was consumed or used directly at its source. This practice was commonly referred to as taking the waters or taking the cure. Locations where mineral water was accessed were known as spas, baths, or wells. The term spa was used when the water was both consumed and used for bathing, bath referred to locations where the water was primarily used for bathing but not consumed, and well described sites where the water was consumed but not used for bathing. These mineral water sites often became popular tourist destinations, even in ancient times, as seen in places like Bath, England. Over time, such locations developed into spa towns or hydropathic hotels, which were often referred to as Hydros. In modern times, it is much more common for mineral water to be bottled directly at its source and distributed for consumption. Traveling to the source of the water to access it directly has become rare and, in many cases, is no longer possible due to exclusive commercial ownership of the water sources. Today, there are over 3,000 brands of mineral water available for purchase worldwide. According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), mineral water is defined as water that contains at least 250 parts per million (ppm) of total dissolved solids (TDS). Additionally, it must come from a source that is accessed through one or more boreholes or springs and must originate from a geologically and physically protected underground water source. No minerals may be artificially added to water classified as mineral water.
